articles.title: A teacher went on a blind date with a surgeon in 1969 and ended up learning to run his dairy farm; their 160-acre Illinois property is now a nature preserve
articles.summary: In February 1969, Beth Temple agreed to meet a surgeon she had never met after colleagues decided the two might suit each other.
articles.body: In February 1969, Beth Temple agreed to meet a surgeon she had never met after colleagues decided the two might suit each other. Beth was a young mother and teacher. Dr Arvid Temple was an older doctor with a dairy farm in eastern Will County, Illinois, which he had bought several years earlier. They married that May, and the farm gradually became part of their shared life. Arvid died in 2007, but Beth continued returning to the property and caring for it. As reported by Forest Preserve District of Will County, more than half a century after their first meeting, the 160-acre Tempest Farm is being protected for the future. The first 40 acres were donated to the Forest Preserve District in 2020, while the remaining 120 acres are under a conservation easement, with full transfer anticipated in the years ahead.How a blind date led Beth to Arvid Temple and Tempest FarmBeth's colleagues had a simple idea when they arranged the meeting. They believed their friend, then a young teacher raising a two-year-old child, might get along with Arvid Temple, a surgeon.Reportedly, she agreed to the blind date in February 1969. Three months later, in May, they were married.By then, Arvid already had a strong attachment to a 160-acre property in Washington Township. He had bought the farm in 1965 and called it Tempest Farm, after a horse he had owned and loved before his medical career took him overseas.The farm was not simply a piece of land he happened to own. It became the setting for much of the couple's life together, particularly at weekends. Beth eventually learned the practical work that came with it, from milking cattle and maintaining buildings to operating machinery and working with tools. She also planted nearly all the trees around the farm buildings, apart from one.The childhood roots of Arvid Temple’s connection to farmingArvid's relationship with land went back to childhood. His parents had emigrated from Belarus, where Jewish people faced restrictions on owning land, and settled in Chicago. Their home had a small backyard shaded by cherry trees, leaving little useful space for growing plants. That modest garden seems to have stayed with him. When he was later able to buy property of his own, he chose a dairy farm.His first horse, Tempest, had a particular place in his memory. He had to sell the animal when he served as a doctor with the US Army during the Korean War in 1951. Later, he reused the name for another horse and even for a large German shepherd that Beth remembered as something of a lovable nuisance.Arvid's route into medicine had not been straightforward either. He was unable to enter some Chicago medical schools because of restrictions on Jewish enrollment at the time. He eventually gained admission to Chicago Medical School, then served in the Army before moving into surgical training at veterans hospitals. That led to a medical career spanning about five decades.Beth turned farm produce into help for local familiesFor Beth, learning the farm was part of learning the life she had chosen with Arvid. She milked cows, worked with a front-end loader and skill saw, tended crops and vegetables and helped keep the dairy buildings clean.There were less pleasant lessons, too. On one occasion, she was kicked by a cow while treating an infected teat. Another involved cleaning the milking barn so thoroughly that she accidentally removed the smells the cattle used to identify their usual places at the stanchions. The cows did not take kindly to the change. It took about two hours to get them settled back into their usual positions.The couple also grew food that they passed on to people who needed it. Some of the produce went to Respond Now, a social service organisation serving people in the Chicago Heights area. For Beth, that work reflected something she had learned from her husband. Arvid, she said, had shown her the importance of looking after other people.After Arvid’s death, Beth continued her life at Tempest FarmArvid died in July 2007, but Beth continued to spend time at Tempest Farm. After his death, she took on a project inside the old chicken coop. With help from friends who worked as carpenters, she began stripping out and reorganising the building. The work took around five years. It eventually became a workshop and storage space, holding gardening and woodworking equipment, automotive supplies, crafting materials and other tools. There is also a warm area for the farm's cats. Photographs of Arvid and reminders of his medical career remain inside.Beth still uses the building in winter, when a portable heater allows her to paint, make toys or read the newspaper. During warmer months, she tends to stop there only for lunch before heading back outside. The farm continues to hold reminders of the couple's years together. The buildings, trees and working spaces are physical traces of a life that was shared there for decades.How 160 acres of Tempest Farm are being preserved for the futureThe first 40 acres of Tempest Farm were donated to the Forest Preserve District in 2020, with the intention that the land would remain protected permanently. The remaining 120 acres, along South Yates Avenue east of Beecher, are under a conservation easement with the Forest Preserve District as beneficiary. Together, the arrangements are expected to make the 160-acre farm the largest land donation in the district's history.The property is more than farmland. Trim and Pike creeks cross the site, while wetlands and areas of rich soil provide habitat for a range of wildlife. Among the species found there are salamanders, green frogs, tree frogs, barn swallows and tree swallows.The working farm buildings will also remain part of the property's story. Arvid had gradually modernised parts of the operation, adding metal siding and roofs, improved milk-collection pipes and concrete around the cow yard to prevent cattle from standing in deep mud.The conservation plan is helping preserve Beth and Arvid’s farm legacyBeth sees the conservation arrangement as a way of keeping something of their life together in place. She has described Arvid as a person who listened carefully to others, a quality she considered unusual. His concern for people influenced his medical career, while his concern for those struggling financially was reflected in the food the couple gave away. Environmental protection mattered to him as well.That is why Beth believes he would have supported the decision to protect Tempest Farm rather than see the property eventually surrounded by development. Under the conservation arrangements, its future is intended to remain tied to agriculture, farming or use as a nature preserve. For Beth, that future does not erase the farm's personal history. She still goes there because it is where she and Arvid spent so much of their time together.The blind date in 1969 led to a marriage that lasted until his death in 2007. The farm he bought four years before they met has now become part of the legacy they are leaving behind.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'As one of the largest research universities...': Arizona State responds to federal probe into J-1 visa use after JD Vance says 'something weird is going on'
articles.summary: Arizona State University has defended its hiring practices after the Trump administration launched a federal investigation into the use of J-1 visas at
articles.body: Arizona State University has defended its hiring practices after the Trump administration launched a federal investigation into the use of J-1 visas at nine major US universities, with Vice President JD Vance alleging that the programme was being used to undercut wages for American researchers.ASU said it had hired the talent needed to support its research and academic operations in full compliance with US laws and policies. The university was among nine institutions named by Vance during an October 8 news conference announcing a new federal crackdown on alleged visa fraud.“As one of the largest research universities in the United States, Arizona State University educates more STEM majors than any other university, and employs one of the largest technical and scientific workforces in the country,” the university said in a statement. “This benefits both the Arizona and the United States economies, and in doing so, ASU has hired the talent needed to perform these functions, and done so in complete compliance with existing United States policy and law.”The investigation is part of a broader Trump administration effort to scrutinise the use of employment and exchange-visitor visa programmes. US Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said subpoenas had already been served and investigations were under way.Why is the US investigating ASU and eight other universities?Vance named Harvard University, Yale University, Stanford University, Brown University, the University of Pittsburgh, the University of California, Davis, the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), ASU and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) as institutions requiring scrutiny.The vice president alleged that the universities relied disproportionately on J-1 visa holders for federally funded research positions, potentially allowing them to pay less than they would pay American graduate students and researchers.According to figures cited by Vance, J-1 visa holders accounted for approximately 61% of research positions supported by federal grants at the nine institutions, compared with a national average of about 38%. He also claimed that American graduate students and researchers earned around $20,000 more than individuals brought in under the J-1 programme.“Something weird is going on at these universities,” Vance said, arguing that the programme was being used to reduce labour costs at the expense of American workers.The allegations have not established that ASU or the other universities violated immigration law. The investigation is intended to examine whether the institutions improperly used visa classifications and federal research funding.What is the J-1 visa programme?The J-1 visa is a non-immigrant visa for individuals participating in designated exchange programmes in the United States. It covers categories including research scholars, professors, students and other exchange visitors.Universities and research institutions use the programme to bring international scholars and researchers to the US for academic exchange, teaching and research.Unlike the H-1B visa, which allows employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations, the J-1 is specifically designed for approved exchange-visitor activities. Its rules and eligibility requirements differ from those governing H-1B employment.The Trump administration's investigation focuses on whether universities have used the J-1 programme in ways that circumvent employment obligations, depress wages or improperly benefit from taxpayer-funded research.D’Esposito said the government would examine whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships or visa-related misconduct had compromised federally funded research.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bipartisan bill barring U.S. purchase of Russian oil on the horizon: Fitzpatrick
articles.summary: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) announced on Saturday he would be introducing a bipartisan bill aimed at stopping President Trump from lifting sanctions on Russian oil amid global fuel shortages. “We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil. It will be called the ‘Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,’”…
articles.body:
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) announced on Saturday he would be introducing a bipartisan bill aimed at stopping President Trump from lifting sanctions on Russian oil amid global fuel shortages.

“We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil. It will be called the ‘Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,’” Fitzpatrick wrote on social media, although it is currently unclear who the Democratic sponsors for the legislation are.

He added that he will force a vote on the bill through a discharge petition and that he believes “it will overwhelmingly” pass.

“I’ve already agreed to be an original cosponsor,” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) wrote on social media . “Congress must make a stand.”

Trump’s deal, which was announced Friday, permits Russia to supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and the global marketplace. Moscow already confirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum to the U.S. and global markets, Russian President Vladimir Putin said in a statement, according to Russian state media.

On Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned the deal signaled to Russia that “it could simply keep attacking” his country. Trump responded, telling reporters outside the White House that Zelensky “could have settled this war many times,” but “chose not to.”

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” the president continued.

The deal drew criticism from both sides of the aisle, including Rep. Gabe Amo (D-R.I.), who sits on the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

“After signing a law to ramp up sanctions on Russia, Trump is paying Putin for oil to deal with the high gas prices caused by his choice of war with Iran? That’s not punishing Putin, that’s profit,” Amo wrote on social media , adding, “Make it make sense.”

In 2022, Congress passed a bill to ban the imports of Russian oil and authorize further sanctions but it contained an exception for the president to allow energy that was already purchased before the legislation passed, or in cases where the importation would be in the national interest.

articles.title: Understand, don't just hear out a child in conflict with law: CJI
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant Saturday said a child in conflict with law must not only be heard but also be understood, since few young
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant Saturday said a child in conflict with law must not only be heard but also be understood, since few young people can speak up for themselves before the police or any authority.Speaking on 10 years of the framing of Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, Kant said very often, the child in conflict with law today was, only a little earlier, a child in need of care and protection whom we did not reach in time and that should be kept in mind while dealing with them."Our answer to such a predicament is restoration, not retribution. The Act presumes everyone below 18 to be innocent of any criminal intent, treats institutional care as a last resort, encourages diversion from formal proceedings, and prefers counselling, community service, and probation to confinement, while promising a fresh start. These choices flow from the Constitutional philosophy discernible from Articles 15(3) and 39 and also from the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which looks to the young assuming a constructive role in society. The 2015 Act thus makes a wager that a child given a second chance is far more likely to become a productive member of society than one branded as a criminal," he said.Supreme Court judge, Justice B V Nagarathna, who is heading SC's Juvenile Justice Committee, said adults have a duty to understand the anxieties of children. "We cannot be dismissive of their concerns, lest they feel alienated and rejected. The true measure of a society and its elders lies in how they deal with their children. We must ensure that we do not fail on that count. All children are ours and their distress is our distress too," Nagarathna said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: SIR stir: 'Kashmir model' in Delhi, situation akin to Emergency, says opposition
articles.summary: Internet restrictions and arrests during Cockroach Janta Party-led anti-SIR protests in New Delhi triggered sharp political reactions Saturday, as J&K CM
articles.body: Internet restrictions and arrests during Cockroach Janta Party-led anti-SIR protests in New Delhi triggered sharp political reactions Saturday, as J&K CM Omar Abdullah said the "Kashmir model" had reached the capital, PDP chief Mehbooba Mufti called the restrictions a reminder of Kashmir's 2019 lockdown, and CPM described the atmosphere as "akin to the Emergency".Omar said the "Kashmir model has been exported to Delhi. Welcome to the New Delhi, modelled on New Jammu & Kashmir." Deputy CM Surinder Choudhary questioned whether the situation was any less serious than during the Emergency and called for chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. National Conference spokesperson Sarah Hayat Shah said New Delhi was witnessing "barely .1% of what was done to Kashmir on Aug 5, 2019."Former CM Mehbooba Mufti called the crackdown "a chilling reminder of Kashmir after the unconstitutional" abrogation of Article 370. "People were locked in their homes, the internet was shut down, and an entire region was placed under siege," she said, recalling her detention for 14 months after Centre revoked J&K's special status and split it into two Union territories in Aug 2019.Leh Apex Body member and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk gave govt 24 hours to release those detained during the New Delhi protest, warning he could launch a sit-in, hunger strike or march in Leh or the capital city."It appears an undeclared emergency has been imposed across the country," he said, urging govt to resolve the dispute through dialogue.In Punjab, CM Bhagwant Mann slammed Union govt over the detentions. "Where is democracy? Around 80,000 to 90,000 security personnel have been deployed. It is only short of deploying Army to stop them. They are students, they are unarmed. They have come for the sake democracy so that their votes are not deleted... if Gen-Z is coming forward, they should be allowed. Why is Centre scared of Jantar Mantar now?" he said.AAP workers, led by Punjab party in charge Manish Sisodia, held a "vote chori" protest against Kumar outside the chief electoral officer's office in Chandigarh. "If Narendra Modi were genuinely popular and had won elections honestly, he would not be afraid of a few young people sitting at Jantar Mantar. But he is afraid because he has become PM by stealing votes, deleting genuine voters and adding fake votes," Sisodia alleged.In Chennai, DMK president and former Tamil Nadu CM MK Stalin condemned the detention of politicians and students protesting against SIR, while Kumar continued to enjoy Z+ security. "Barricading #Delhi, shutting down the internet and detaining politicians cannot crush the uprising of India's youth," he said, demanding Kumar's removal, a halt to SIR and the release of detainees.In Keralam, CPM condemned the detentions as creating an atmosphere "akin to the Emergency" and accused Delhi police of acting like "RSS-BJP goons". Top CPM functionaries along with MPs and functionaries of the party's women's, student and youth wings were detained while trying to join the Jantar Mantar protest. CPM called for demonstrations across Keralam.Congress general secretary KC Venugopal accused PM Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah of protecting Kumar at political cost. articles.title: In 2006, Jackie Chan asked fans to help build schools one dollar at a time and promised to match their gifts; six years later, their combined contributions had passed $192,000 for children in rural China
articles.summary: Jackie Chan’s appeal was simple: if fans could spare a dollar, he would match it and put both contributions towards building schools for children in
articles.body: Jackie Chan’s appeal was simple: if fans could spare a dollar, he would match it and put both contributions towards building schools for children in remote parts of China. The “Build a School for a Dollar” project turned small gifts into a shared effort, inviting children and adults around the world to contribute whatever they could. According to the project’s page on Jackie’s Kids Corner, over six years fans donated more than $96,000, and Chan matched their gifts, bringing the combined total to more than $192,000. The money was enough to build several schools in poor and remote areas. The campaign’s idea was modest, but its promise was powerful: no contribution was too small to become part of something larger.A dollar that became twoChan’s promise was to match donations dollar for dollar. A fan who gave one dollar would effectively contribute two, while someone who gave ten dollars would see that gift doubled. The project’s organisers stressed that contributions could come in any amount and from any country.That open invitation helped give the campaign its character. It was not presented as a fundraising drive reserved for wealthy donors. Children could send pocket money, and adults could contribute spare change or a larger sum. The point was participation as much as the size of any single gift.The project was connected to the Dragon’s Heart Foundation, which worked to help children in poor and remote parts of China. Building a school required more than the money raised by fans. The project page noted that a school cost about $75,000, with the Chinese government providing the rest of the construction funding. Chan’s match helped close the gap and make the target more achievable.From fan contributions to schoolsThe campaign began in 2006, asking supporters to help finance school construction through small donations. The fundraising model made the goal easier to understand: if fans together raised $37,500, Chan’s matching donation would bring the total to the $75,000 needed for a school.The project’s early updates showed how the gifts accumulated. In 2008, Jackie Chan’s Kids Corner reported that fans had raised nearly $40,000 in less than two years. With Chan matching their donations, the combined sum had reached the amount needed to finance a school.The initiative did not stop after the first target. Fans continued contributing, and the project page later reported that their donations had passed $96,000 over six years. Chan’s matching gifts brought the overall total above $192,000, enough to build several schools in poor and remote areas.That progress made the campaign more than a one-time appeal. Each new donation helped move the effort towards another school, while the matching promise gave contributors a clear reason to believe their money would have twice the impact.A global effort with a personal touchThe project page invited supporters to send money in whatever currency they used. A donation did not need to be a US dollar bill, and the appeal welcomed contributions in different amounts. That flexibility helped make the initiative accessible to a global fan base.Supporters also found ways to make the fundraising personal. Jackie Chan’s Kids Corner described fans donating money in place of birthday gifts, while fan gatherings and community events helped raise contributions. In one account, a supporter said friends and family gave to the school project instead of bringing presents.That spirit matched Chan’s broader message about generosity. In an April 2013 diary entry, he recalled asking children around the world to donate pocket money or spare change, even if it was only one dollar. He said he would match every donation and direct the combined funds to charity.For fans, the campaign offered a way to take part in a cause linked to someone they admired. Chan’s fame helped draw attention, but the project’s structure gave people a tangible role: each small gift joined a growing total intended for school construction.Building opportunity in remote areasA school building can represent more than a place to attend lessons. In remote communities, access to education may depend on whether a school exists close enough for children to reach it. A local classroom can give students a regular place to learn, meet teachers and build the foundations for future opportunities.The project’s focus on poor and remote areas of China reflected that practical need. By directing funds towards school construction, the campaign aimed to create lasting infrastructure rather than provide only short-term assistance.The $192,000 figure reported by the project page was a combined amount, including both fan donations and Chan’s matching contributions. It was enough to build several schools, according to the campaign. The project did not claim that donations alone covered every expense. Instead, it described a partnership in which fan gifts, Chan’s match and government construction funding helped make the buildings possible.A lesson in givingThe campaign also carried a message beyond its fundraising target. Chan said the project was about teaching people how to give and care, and about bringing people from different places together through a shared effort. Small donations could become a lesson in generosity when they were joined with contributions from thousands of others.That approach helps explain why the one-dollar idea endured. It made philanthropy feel possible for people who might otherwise assume they had too little to offer. The promise to match each contribution also made the impact easy to understand, giving a modest gift a visible role in the larger goal.Six years after Chan first asked fans to help, their donations had exceeded $96,000, and his matching gifts brought the combined amount above $192,000. The campaign turned that sum into funding for several schools in rural China. Its legacy is not just the buildings, but the idea they share: a small act of generosity can grow when people choose to contribute together.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Philadelphia police officer killed, another wounded after responding to reports of man with a gun
articles.summary: A Philadelphia police officer was killed and a second was shot a dozen times after responding to a report of a man with a gun early Saturday, officials said.
articles.body: A Philadelphia police officer was killed and a second was shot a dozen times after responding to a report of a man with a gun early Saturday, officials said. Shane Seiber, 40, and the other officer were transported to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center and underwent surgery, according to Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel. The surviving officer, who was shot 12 times, is in stable condition, Bethel said. Authorities are charging Eric Lewis, 35, with homicide in the killing, according to Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner. Lewis also faces other charges, including attempted homicide in the shooting of the other officer and nine others who responded to the scene, Krasner said. None of those nine were injured. He is being held without bail and will be arraigned soon, Krasner said. Lewis was previously convicted of criminal offenses including assault, theft and carrying a firearm publicly, according to court records. Seiber was a 10-year veteran of the police department. Gov. Josh Shapiro said he ordered flags to fly at half-staff for Seiber, who is survived by his wife and two children — a 7-year-old boy and a 3-year-old girl. “This is a brutal, senseless, horrific killing,” Krasner said.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Unprecedented security arrangements from central Delhi to the borders, phalanxes of 35,000 police and paramilitary personnel and a virtual choke on metro services and trains foiled Cockroach Janta Party's march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday. The city, however, remained on edge, with young protesters being detained on their way to the protest site and bundled into buses and vans, kicking and screaming, through the day.With CJP's Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das detained at the airport, the outfit's national organisation in-charge, Ajinkya Shinde, was named to lead the protests. The computer science grad, a former AAP worker, said protests would continue till Gyanesh Kumar resigned as CEC.With top CJP functionaries being kept away from Jantar Mantar, small groups dodged security personnel and staged flash protests at Safdarjung flyover, Dilli Haat and Gurdwara Bangla Sahib complex, among other places.The impromptu gathering near Safdarjung flyover by AISA national president Neha Bora, lawyer Prashant Bhushan, political commentator Yogendra Yadav, and several others caught police off-guard momentarily around 1pm. The protesters were eventually detained.It was obvious since Thursday that the call by CJP, supported by some political outfits, for a protest against the CEC and SIR at Jantar Mantar at 10am on Saturday would be met with stiff resistance. New Delhi was divided into 20 zones, with 1-2 companies of CAPF and Delhi Police deployed at every nook and corner. BSF was also present at the city's borders. Security arrangements may not see let-up todayWater cannons and tear-gas vehicles were kept ready. Multiple layers of barricades were erected and police personnel closely questioned people heading towards the New Delhi area, particularly in the direction of Jantar Mantar. Police said there were only some isolated incidents of minor confrontations. While three or four personnel, including women, were injured in incidents of stone-pelting and other skirmishes, a DCP fractured his hand, they said.Police claimed they had detained 2,500 people in the city — 600-700 people on stretches leading to Jantar Mantar, and others from different parts of Delhi, including the borders. The police figures were, however, hotly contested, with sources saying around 7,000 people were detained, counting those who were not allowed to leave their homes and were put under preventive detention.CJP’s Ajinkya Shinde, who will lead the protests now, alleged more than 15,000 people, including students, civil society members and political functionaries, had been illegally detained across the country. An undeclared emergency had been imposed in Delhi, he said.Police said apart from the fact that permission had not been given for the protest, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) were in force, making the proposed gathering illegal.Four former chief ministers — Aam Aadmi Party convener Arvind Kejriwal, Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee, Kerala’s Pinarayi Vijayan, and Manik Sarkar of Tripura — were detained. CPM veteran Brinda Karat, Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas, and TMC functionaries Derek O’Brien and Dola Sen were also detained.Detained protesters were taken in buses to Chhatrasal Stadium, Rajiv Gandhi Stadium, Yamuna Sports Complex and Surajmal Stadium, all designated earlier for this purpose. Around 600 buses, including some from Third Battalion used to transport prisoners, were used to ferry those detained.Around 9pm, police claimed they had released everyone, but refused to respond when asked about Dipke, Ranka and Das. Multiple cases will be registered in connection with violation of prohibitory orders and assault, besides other sections, police said.With CJP sources saying they will continue their protests and Congress and other INDIA bloc parties planning a march in the city Monday, the security paraphernalia is likely to remain in place for the next few days.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: While today's freezers are packed with ice cream flavors such as cookies and cream, salted caramel and mint chocolate chip, some old-time favorites seem to have melted away. Flavors including Butter Brickle, rum raisin and maple walnut were once familiar options at ice cream counters and grocery stores, but many have become harder to find as tastes have changed. articles.title: MPs attempt to overturn ruling which protects police from being sued
articles.summary: MPs are seeking to stop immunity applying when police fabricate evidence or are dishonest or negligent.
articles.body:
Backbench MPs are seeking to roll back a court ruling they say will have "devastating consequences" for victims of crime by preventing them taking legal action against the police, even when there have been grave investigative failings.

The 2025 Court of Appeal judgment, which applies to England and Wales, held that police officers are immune from civil litigation both in their role as witnesses, and for conduct or statements they make when carrying out criminal investigations.

Conservative Andrew Mitchell and Labour's Jess Phillips have submitted an amendment to a bill being debated in Parliament next week seeking to counteract the ruling.

Separately, the judgment could also be overturned at a Supreme Court appeal this month.

The MPs are seeking to stop immunity applying, including in cases where police have fabricated evidence, been dishonest or negligent, and where there has been a reckless disclosure of confidential information relating to victims.

The ruling came in a case brought by a victim of serious domestic violence who fled her abuser for a secret refuge, but Sussex Police included her new address in a file sent to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) without sufficiently flagging its confidentiality.

A CPS lawyer subsequently disclosed her address in court during a bail hearing, thereby revealing it to her abuser. As a result, she had to flee again.

The woman said the disclosure of her address had meant the place she was supposed to be safe "no longer felt safe at all" and she was still living with the impact of what happened and that loss of security.

She brought claims against both the police and CPS, arguing their failure placed her in fear for her life, compelled her to leave her home, caused her to suffer loss of earnings, and resulted in her developing a psychiatric injury. Her claims were initially rejected, reinstated on appeal, then struck out again.

The key issue was who could be held legally responsible for what happened, and who would benefit from legal immunity. Witnesses and lawyers have what is known as "core immunity" for things they say in court, so that they can speak freely there.

The Court of Appeal ruling further expanded such immunity, holding that it extends to an extremely broad range of police activity, including conduct or statements which are part of an investigation leading to a potential prosecution

Most types of legal claim are thus blocked by this immunity, including cases about serious human rights abuses and data breaches, and there are no exemptions for unjustifiable conduct.

Officers can still be prosecuted in the criminal courts and held accountable by police misconduct processes.

The amendment by Mitchell and Phillips, which will be debated on Tuesday, states that, except while acting as witnesses, no immunity applies to actions by police officers in preparation for criminal proceedings, including in cases where there are specified grave failings.

Mitchell told BBC News the "police misconduct immunity created by the Court of Appeal's ruling" was extremely concerning and that if "we fail to close this legal loophole there will be devastating consequences for victims".

He cited the case of Ali Kololo, saying his life was "ruined by a wrongful conviction secured, in large part, by the Metropolitan Police".

Mr Kololo, a Kenyan woodcutter, spent 11 years in jail after being wrongfully convicted of assisting a gang that attacked two British tourists in Kenya in 2011 - one of whom was murdered. He was sentenced to death following a trial in Kenya, at which a senior Met officer who was called to appear as a prosecution witness omitted key evidence.

Mr Kololo - who is represented by human rights group, Reprieve - is suing the Met, but the force has said it will rely on the legal principle of core immunity in defending the claim, a position likely to be bolstered by the Court of Appeal ruling.

A Met spokesperson said the force would not comment on the ongoing civil claim, but said its thoughts were with Mr Kololo, the victims of the crime and their families.

Kate Ellis, from the Centre for Women's Justice, told the BBC forces may now argue they cannot be "held legally responsible at all for serious mistakes made in a criminal investigation" and it could lead to an "accountability gap" where police forces who fail to investigate rapists, stalkers or domestic abusers "face no consequences for their failings".

A government spokesperson said: "The home secretary and lord chancellor commissioned a review into police accountability following long-standing concerns from policing leaders, officers, victims and their families that the current system is not fit for purpose. Any changes to how the police are treated should be considered alongside the wider findings of this review."

Sussex Police and the National Police Chiefs Council both declined to comment at this time.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia says attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 and wounded more than 300
articles.summary: At least 12 people were killed and over 300 injured after a missile struck Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, Saudi
articles.body: At least 12 people were killed and over 300 injured after a missile struck Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said.According to GACA, the fatalities included four Saudi citizens and residents of several other nationalities, including two Bangladeshis and one each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. Some of the injured are in critical condition and are receiving medical treatment at several hospitals.“Further to its earlier statement regarding the attack targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, October 10, 2026, corresponding to 29 Rabi' Al-Thani 1448H, the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) clarifies that the attack resulted in (12) fatalities, including (4) Saudi citizens and residents of the following nationalities: (2) Bangladeshi, (1) American, (1) Egyptian, (1) Jordanian, (1) Syrian, (1) Palestinian and (1) Sudanese," GACA said."The attack also left (309) others injured, including individuals in critical condition. All injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals. May Allah bestow His mercy upon those who lost their lives and grant the injured a speedy recovery. The attack also caused property damage, the extent of which is currently being assessed," the statement added.King Khalid International Airport has been targeted multiple times over the past week, since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen.The incident follows earlier attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport on October 6 and 7, which GACA said had resulted in three deaths and 36 injuries.Following the attack, operations at the airport were temporarily suspended and travellers were evacuated, while dozens of ambulances were seen rushing to the site. This came after the airport issued a brief alert urging passengers to check their flight status with airlines before heading there. According to flight-tracking platform Flightradar24, flights bound for Riyadh were being diverted to other destinations nearly four hours after the last flight landed at 2:05 pm local time.At least 225 flights at King Khalid International Airport had been cancelled over the preceding 24 hours, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware.Meanwhile, the US Embassy in Riyadh said it was aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport and urged American citizens in the Saudi capital to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.The UK Embassy also advised British nationals to stay away from the airport area following what it described as a “serious incident”.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Opposition parties on Saturday lashed out at govt over wide security curbs to foil the Cockroach Janta Party's call for protest at Jantar Mantar but a defiant BJP backed the clampdown, saying Parliament, and not streets, will run the country.BJP president Nitin Nabin alleged two anarchic groups - one of the INDIA bloc and another led by Arvind Kejriwal and his "associate" CJP, were seeking to stoke unrest in the country and were in a battle of one-upmanship over spreading chaos: "They are working in collusion with foreign forces to destabilise India."Congress, which kept away from Saturday's protests, lent its support to the agitating youths and said their "peaceful" stir has left govt rattled and nervous.Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said, "Youth of India, I am proud of you. Keep protesting. We are standing with you. I have been fighting Narendra Modi and the RSS for over a decade now. The core characteristic of these people is cowardice.""Narendra Modi, Amit Shah, Mohan Bhagwat, Gyanesh Kumar and Ajit Doval, the villains of this story, are slowly finding the space closing around them. We are closing that space," he added, claiming that govt may further ramp up security measures but protests over the SIR issue will continue.A combative BJP was, however, categorical that CJP, which had "broken" the conditions under which their members were allowed to launch their stir in July, could not have been allowed to "hijack" Jantar Mantar again. "Democracy has prevailed over anarchy. The country will be governed through Parliament, not the streets. The country cannot be run by spreading anarchy on the streets," Ravi Shankar Prasad said.BJP says protest a flop; oppn puts united frontSpeaking at the sixth edition of his youth outreach programme, 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' at Chennai's Island Grounds, Rahul said "Mogambo Modi" was destroying India's democracy, referring to the PM. "Mr Modi doesn't understand that the game is over," he added. "I want to tell all the students in Delhi, do not worry. Stand up for everything you believe in and never stop asking questions," Gandhi said, asserting, "We are standing with you."SP president Akhilesh Yadav said, "Now, the nation will unite in Delhi! We stand with the youthful energy of the nation. If BJP govt thinks it can halt the people through the might of power, this will prove to be an even greater mistake on its part." Left leaders, including M A Baby of CPM, D Raja of CPI and Dipankar Bhattacharya of CPI(ML), condemned the "widespread repression" unleashed by Delhi Police on peaceful protesters.BJP fielded an array of functionaries to counter the opposition, with Sambit Patra saying the protest turned out to be a flop show by "anarchist forces" and asserting that the national capital cannot be allowed to be held hostage by those stoking disorder.Patra alleged Rahul's show of support to the world's richest person, Elon Musk, over his potshots at the Indian govt's policy is part of his wider efforts, including the campaign against SIR to "help" infiltrators, to draw backing from foreign players to destabilise India and called him Mir Jafar, an 18th-century military commander synonymous with treachery.'Get the latest India News and Live updates.
